demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

vignette:
Layla sits in the armchair across from me, her posture rigid, her hands folded loosely in her lap. At 31, she is the regional social media manager for a lifestyle brand, and I notice she arrives for our sessions directly from work, still carrying the polished veneer she must wear online. The smile she offers is automatic, a practiced upload, but it fades the moment she speaks. “I don’t know how to start,” she says, her accent softening the edges of her words. “Nothing feels real anymore.”

The fracture happened two years ago. She was driving home late from a launch event, exhausted after a seventy-hour week. She glanced at her phone for a single second to silence a notification from a client. When she looked up, a man was in the crosswalk. His name was Amir. He was a sculptor, thirty-four years old, walking home from a gallery opening. “I felt the thud before I understood what it was,” she tells me, her voice dropping to a whisper. “The sound was… wet. I remember screaming, but I couldn’t hear myself.” Amir survived, but the traumatic brain injury and a broken spine permanently altered his life. He will never walk again. He will never hold a chisel. She knows this because she found a GoFundMe page his family set up; she donates to it every month as a quiet, private penance.

Her job now feels like a cruel performance. She spends her days curating a world of aspirational happiness—crafting captions about chasing dreams, road trips, and gratitude. The dissonance is suffocating. “Every morning I schedule posts about living your best life,” she says, “and then I open a browser tab and search for Amir’s name. I am selling a lie that I destroyed for someone else.” She cannot scroll past an image of a car or a bicycle. A client recently pitched a campaign about “life’s journey,” and she excused herself from the meeting, shaking. Her boss has noticed her declining engagement and growing irritability. She has told no one at work what she did.

Her marriage to Rami disintegrated slowly. He tried to hold her up, driving her everywhere since she refuses to get behind the wheel, sitting with her in the dark when the nightmares woke her. But she became a ghost in their home. She couldn’t bear his touch. “I felt like I was contagious,” she explains. “How could I let him love me when I had taken someone else’s life? Not their life, but… their life.” She divorced him six months ago. “It was the only gift I could give him. I couldn’t stand to watch him drown in my guilt with me.”

The symptoms are woven into every hour of her day. She hasn’t driven a car since the accident; she takes two buses and a train to work, walking an extra mile to avoid the exact intersection. The sound of a car horn makes her hit the ground. A colleague’s phone notification recently played the same tone as hers did that night; Layla fled the open office and vomited in the bathroom. She is hypervigilant on every sidewalk, scanning every headlight, every crosswalk. She cannot sleep without the television on, a barrier against the silence that precedes the crash. She feels emotionally hollow. Her friends have stopped calling. “I have nothing to offer,” she says flatly. “I am a black hole. Everything good gets pulled into me and destroyed.”

She tells me she googles Amir every single day. She has never reached out to him—she is too terrified of his answer, or of his forgiveness. She monitors his online presence for any sign of recovery, any sign of suffering. It is her ritual of self-flagellation. She cannot let him go. Letting him go, in her mind, means letting herself off the hook, and she does not believe she deserves that.

Today, in session, I ask her what she wants from our work together. She looks at her hands for a very long time. “I want to stop Googling him,” she whispers. “I want to be able to walk down the street without scanning for threats. I want to know if it’s possible to feel something other than this guilt. I don’t need to be happy. I just need to stop feeling like I am drowning every single second.”

She holds the accident like a sacred text, reading it over and over, searching for the split second she could have chosen differently. She is not yet ready to forgive herself, but she is beginning, slowly, to see that the constant reliving is a form of punishment that serves no one. She is learning the terrifying grammar of the present tense, trying to find a way to live in a world that moved on while she stayed frozen, two years ago, in the moment before the impact.
